summary: Background: Adolescence is a critical period for mental health prevention; yet, many young people face barriers to help-seeking, including stigma, limited mental health literacy, and restricted access to services. Preventive digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) offer a scalable, low-threshold approach to early support, but uptake and sustained engagement remain limited. Existing research has predominantly relied on quantitative methods and has only partly captured adolescents’ perspectives. Qualitative research is therefore needed to inform the design and implementation of preventive DMHIs. Objective: This study aimed to explore adolescents’ perspectives on factors influencing the anticipated uptake, expected engagement, and implementation of preventive transdiagnostic DMHIs across person, intervention, and system levels. Methods: This qualitative study was conducted in Switzerland using a single-interview design in the predesign phase of the development of a transdiagnostic preventive DMHI. Adolescents aged 12‐21 years were recruited through voluntary response sampling via social media and the project website. Semistructured interviews explored experiences with online help-seeking, factors influencing DMHI anticipated uptake and expected engagement, and recommendations for implementation. Interviews were conducted in person or via video call between January and June 2022, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using a hybrid deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis. Intercoder agreement was assessed using Cohen κ (κ=0.72). Results: A total of 48 adolescents (mean age 16.52, SD 2.67 years; 32/48, 72.9% female) participated. In total, 8 main topics and multiple subtopics were identified across person, intervention, system, and cross levels. Person-level factors highlighted the importance of mental health literacy, preuptake communication, and relevance of social networks. Intervention-level factors emphasized usability, personalization, and privacy, while system-level findings reflected expectations for adaptive, integrated, and low-threshold mental health services. Trust and support emerged as cross-level factors for engagement. In addition, participants described several discrepancies between desired intervention characteristics and practical implementation, particularly regarding personalization, anonymity, peer exchange, and human support. Conclusions: Adolescents’ perspectives highlight that successful implementation of preventive DMHIs requires attention beyond intervention design to preuptake communication strategies, mental health literacy promotion, and integration within adaptive care systems. The tension between adolescents’ desire for immediate human-delivered support and the self-guided nature of preventive DMHIs underscores the need for clear clinical boundaries and explicit escalation pathways.
title: Adolescents’ Perspectives on Uptake, Engagement, and Implementation to Inform the Development of a Preventive Transdiagnostic Digital Mental Health Intervention: Qualitative Interview Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> To cope with the challenges of digital transformation in health and well-being, people need digital health literacy (DHL), namely the competencies to access, understand, appraise, and apply digital health–related information and services for their own and others’ health and well-being. So far, however, there have been no data on the level of DHL in Switzerland. <strong>Objective:</strong> As part of the international Health Literacy Survey 2019-2021 (HLS<sub>19</sub>), this study aimed to close this gap by investigating DHL, the population groups particularly affected by low DHL, its health-related consequences, as well as use of digital information sources in the general population in Switzerland. <strong>Methods:</strong> Participants were recruited from the Swiss Federal Statistical Office sampling frame using stratification by linguistic region, age, and gender. Of the 4764 individuals contacted, 2554 completed the survey (response rate: 53.6%). Responses from 52 participants were excluded because fewer than 80% of the general health literacy items had been completed. Additionally, 168 participants from the overall study sample were excluded from the calculation of the digital health literacy score (HL-DIGI) because of insufficient completion of the DHL items. DHL of 2334 people was assessed between March and April 2020 with an online questionnaire. Descriptive statistical analysis, Pearson chi-square tests, Spearman rank correlations, and multivariable linear regression analyses were performed to examine DHL and its associations with sociodemographic characteristics, health-related consequences, and use of digital information sources. <strong>Results:</strong> Most of the respondents report inadequate (1034/2334, 44.3%) or problematic (651/2334, 27.9%) DHL levels. DHL resulted to be negatively associated with older age (B=−0.278, 95% CI −0.371 to −0.185), greater financial deprivation (B=−0.101, 95% CI −0.148 to −0.054) and migration background (B=−5.992, 95% CI −8.990 to −2.994), and positively associated with education in the health sector (B=11.337, 95% CI 7.720 to 14.953) and social support (B=1.109, 95% CI 0.308 to 1.909). In addition, lower educational attainment was associated with lower DHL scores compared with having a master’s degree or higher. Higher DHL was associated with better self-assessed general health status (odds ratio [OR] 1.005, 95% CI 1.003-1.007), improved self-management (OR 0.989, 95% CI 0.984-0.993), and lower likelihood of experiencing restrictions of usual activities due to health problems (OR 1.004, 95% CI 1.001-1.007). Furthermore, people with higher DHL tend to rely more on face-to-face information from health care professionals and to use digital sources less frequently. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> This study offers first insights into the DHL of the population in Switzerland and indicates that almost three-quarters (72.2%) of the population have low DHL. These results are in line with those of other European countries and clearly show the urgency of measures to improve DHL, especially among vulnerable population groups.
title: Health Literacy in the Age of Digitalization in Switzerland: Cross-Sectional Representative Study

summary: Background: In health systems, AI is increasingly being implemented as a form of clinical decision support (CDS). Research on patient perspectives, however, lags behind clinician-focused studies. Before the introduction of AI-based tools, clinicians often used and continue to use rule-based guidelines and risk calculators (RCs) to inform decision-making. Prior research has shown that RCs for CDS have mixed effects on patient adherence to treatment recommendations, whereas for AI-based tools, the effect is still not clear. Objective: This study aims to assess differences in patients’ behavioral intentions, trust, and preferences for clinical recommendations provided by doctors alone, doctors supported by RCs, and doctors supported by AI-based risk predictions. We also evaluate how sociodemographic characteristics affect these perceptions. Methods: We surveyed 1185 US-based adults. Participants rated their likelihood of taking recommended clinical actions (behavioral intentions) across 6 clinical scenarios, where they were randomized to a different recommendation source (doctor, doctor + RC, and doctor + AI). Participants also rated their trust in the recommendation, indicated their preferred source for recommendations, and provided qualitative feedback. Results: Behavioral intentions differed by recommendation source such that the doctor + RC condition had greater odds of behavioral intention than the doctor + AI condition. Behavioral intentions were also affected by the clinical condition. Participants had greater odds of trusting doctors alone over doctor + RC, and both doctors alone and doctor + RC had greater trust than doctor + AI. However, a plurality of participants ultimately preferred a doctor using an RC for making recommendations. Several sociodemographic differences were detected, namely, participants with higher subjective numeracy and literacy had higher odds of taking clinical action and higher trust across decision-support sources. We detected qualitative themes in the following categories: decision quality and reliability; trust and perceptions; patient-centeredness and autonomy; fairness, transparency, and ethics. Across categories, participants reported skepticism toward all decision sources and potential misunderstanding of AI’s ability to personalize risk predictions. Some participants also stated that they had no additional concerns or were uncertain regarding their feelings. Conclusions: These findings reveal novel, nuanced patient preferences shaped by task and context, offering guidance for aligning AI-supported care with patient values. Patients were not aligned on the recommendation source across intentions, trust, and preferences. Taken together, our results indicate that patients prefer doctors working with easy-to-understand, explainable support but are still learning to trust these tools. Our findings also highlight the continued importance of the clinical context and its interaction with computer-assisted decision support. Future work should evaluate how we can transparently convey to patients the use of AI in clinical decision-making, embedded within the given clinical context. This may present an opportunity to bolster, rather than erode, patient trust.
title: Investigating Patient Trust and Intention to Act in AI-Supported Clinical Decisions: Cross-Sectional Survey

summary: Clinical AI governance has advanced rapidly in technical validation, regulatory compliance, risk management, human oversight, and postdeployment monitoring. Yet a more fundamental question often remains implicit: under what conditions are health institutions justified in exercising consequential authority through AI over patients, clinicians, and communities? In this Viewpoint, we argue that legitimacy should be recognized as an independent governance requirement, distinct from technical assurance, legal and ethical compliance, trust, acceptance, and institutional approval. Our aim is to distinguish institutional approval from public authorization and to propose a normative framework for authorizing consequential clinical AI deployments. We address health system leaders, clinical AI governance and procurement teams, frontline clinicians, and patient and community representatives. Drawing on theories of legitimacy and public value and published clinical AI governance research, we make the following contributions: (1) the concept of the unclaimed decision, defined as a consequential choice about purpose, threshold, population, or priority for which no actor clearly assumes responsibility for public justification; (2) a tripartite framework comprising procedural authorization, substantive justification, and relational renewal; and (3) practical governance tools to support public justification, contestation, and renewal. These tools include 3 minimum auditable conditions: visibility of deployment; affected-party input before governing conditions are fixed; and conditional reviewability, which requires a predefined trigger that can be invoked by a named actor outside the deploying team. A 5-question public authorization test examines purpose, distribution, exclusion, meaningful choice and contestability, and renewal. Governance intensity should increase with clinical consequence; distributive reach; difficulty of reversal; and the absence of genuine, informed choice. For smaller health care organizations, we propose ways to perform the same core governance functions through existing advisory bodies, targeted interviews, shared regional resources, and standardized documentation. We also outline a heuristic for identifying affected publics, procedures for specifying participation authority and resolving disagreement, and procurement provisions that preserve reviewability across vendor boundaries. These are normative proposals requiring evaluation. Public authorization requires continuing substantive justification; it cannot be inferred from compliance, popularity, or completion of an audit checklist.
title: Institutional Approval Is Not Public Authorization: Legitimacy as a Governance Requirement for Clinical AI

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Female university students encounter appearance ideals, comparison cues, and appearance-related pressure across traditional and digital media environments. These sociocultural influences may coexist with psychological resources such as body appreciation and weight-control self-efficacy. However, variable-centered analyses may obscure heterogeneity in how these characteristics are combined within individuals. The measures used in this study assessed broader sociocultural appearance-related attitudes rather than platform-specific digital exposure. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to identify latent profiles characterized by ideal-body internalization, appearance comparison, perceived media pressure, body appreciation, and weight-control self-efficacy among female university students and to examine whether these profiles differed in moderate-intensity exercise duration, self-perceived body size, and screen-based sedentary behavior. <strong>Methods:</strong> A cross-sectional online survey was conducted between May and June 2025 among 2034 female students recruited by convenience sampling from 1 comprehensive university in China. Latent profile analysis compared 1- through 6-profile solutions. Model selection considered information criteria, likelihood-ratio tests, entropy, profile size, parsimony, and substantive interpretability. Distal outcomes were compared using the Bolck-Croon-Hagenaars (BCH) procedure for continuous outcomes and the distal categorical outcome (DCAT) procedure for categorical outcomes. Sensitivity analyses examined alternative exercise definitions, transformations, extreme-value handling, sociodemographic adjustment, and self-reported BMI. Conventionally calculated weekly moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) outcomes were examined among 1056 participants with complete activity data. The primary analysis preserved classification uncertainty, and supplementary models assessed the robustness of associations without treating most-likely profile membership as error-free. No population-prevalence inference was intended. <strong>Results:</strong> A 4-profile solution was retained (entropy=0.874): very low sociocultural attitudes—higher body appreciation (137/2034, 6.74%), average sociocultural attitudes (1081/2034, 53.15%), lower sociocultural attitudes (452/2034, 22.22%), and higher sociocultural attitudes (364/2034, 17.9%). Solutions with 5 and 6 profiles each contained a very small class of approximately 1.7% (35/2034), and the adjusted Lo-Mendell-Rubin test comparing 6 vs 5 profiles was nonsignificant (<i>P</i>=.47). The profiles were differentiated primarily by a low-to-high gradient in appearance comparison, ideal-body internalization, and perceived media pressure. Moderate-intensity exercise duration differed across profiles in the primary analysis (BCH Wald <i>χ</i><sup>2</sup><sub>3</sub>=15.3; <i>P</i>=.002), but complete-case weekly MVPA did not (<i>P</i>=.52). Body-size perception differed in the unadjusted analysis (DCAT <i>χ</i><sup>2</sup><sub>9</sub>=20.4; <i>P</i>=.02), although the overall association was not independent of sociodemographic characteristics and self-reported BMI. Weekly screen-use categories did not differ significantly across profiles (DCAT <i>χ</i><sup>2</sup><sub>12</sub>=16.7; <i>P</i>=.16). <strong>Conclusions:</strong> The retained profiles were sample-specific statistical configurations that largely represented a sociocultural low-to-high gradient rather than 4 clearly discrete psychological types. Associations with exercise and body-size perception were modest and sensitive to outcome definition or covariate adjustment. The cross-sectional findings do not establish causal direction or digital media mechanisms. Longitudinal, multisite studies incorporating direct measures of digital exposure, exercise motivation, objectively assessed activity, and measured anthropometry are needed.
title: Sociocultural Appearance-Related Attitudes and Psychological Resources and Their Associations With Moderate-Intensity Exercise, Body Size Perception, and Screen Time Among Female University Students: Cross-Sectional Latent Profile Analysis

summary: Background: Bipolar disorder (BP) affects 1% to 3% of adults worldwide, with diagnostic delays averaging 6 years and high initial misdiagnosis rates. The absence of objective diagnostic measures contributes to clinical uncertainty and suboptimal outcomes. Objective: This study aimed to (1) develop a machine learning model for BP diagnosis and mood state classification using linguistic and acoustic features, (2) identify features associated with different mood states by comparing each with healthy controls (HC), and (3) explore whether features distinguish between mood states within BP. Methods: We analyzed data prospectively collected over 7 years from 61 patients with BP and 99 HC across Japan. Speech samples were collected via semistructured interviews over 1 to 5 visits and analyzed cross-sectionally, using aggregated or single-visit observations per participant rather than within-person longitudinal modeling. We extracted 6373 acoustic features (openSMILE 3.0, ComParE 2016) and 211 linguistic features. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)–regularized logistic regression with nested cross-validation and age- and sex-matched undersampling was used. Mood states were classified as depressive state (DS; Hamilton Depression Rating Scale-17 [HAMD-17] ≥8, Young Mania Rating Scale [YMRS] ≤7), state with manic/mixed symptoms (MS/MX; YMRS ≥8), or euthymic state (ES; HAMD-17 ≤7, YMRS ≤7). Seven classification tasks included BP vs HC, each mood state vs HC, and interstate comparisons. Feature importance was validated via permutation testing (<.05). Medication sensitivity analyses were performed. Results: The model achieved high discrimination for BP vs HC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]=0.916, 95% CI 0.854‐0.958; sensitivity 0.933; specificity 0.859) and strong performance for mood states vs HC (AUC=0.805‐0.874). Acoustic features comprised 96% to 98% of the features achieving statistical significance (<.05), including mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, spectral characteristics, and voice quality measures, showing strong correlations with diagnostic probabilities (|ρ|=0.35‐0.85) and symptom severity (HAMD-17: ρ=–0.51; YMRS: ρ=–0.37); 2 to 4 linguistic features per comparison also reached significance. With sample independence ensured for interstate comparisons, DS vs ES significantly exceeded chance (AUC=0.760, permutation =.03), whereas MS/MX vs ES (AUC=0.601, =.20) and DS vs MS/MX (AUC=0.569, =.30) did not, suggesting that markers primarily reflect persistent disease characteristics with partial state-associated components in depressive states. Conclusions: The combined acoustic-linguistic model, driven primarily by acoustic features, shows potential as an objective aid for BP diagnosis (AUC>0.9), largely free of medication confounding; some features remained detectable during euthymia, although ES discrimination could not be fully separated from concurrent antipsychotic treatment. Although DS showed partial distinguishability from ES, overall limitations remain for monitoring mood state changes. Findings require validation in diverse populations and against other psychiatric conditions.
title: Machine Learning Classification of Bipolar Disorder Across Mood States Using Natural Language Processing and Speech Analysis: Observational Study
